Yes. 

The story uses rich subtext that significantly enhances the setting rather than feeling forced. On the surface, the narrator is simply describing his cramped cabin, the noisy promenade deck, and his decision to sleep during the day to avoid the other passengers. However, the subtext—conveyed through metaphors like referring to the cabin as a "muffige Grab" (musty grave) and "kleinen Sarg" (little coffin), or the ship's engine as the "atmende Herz des Leviathans" (breathing heart of the Leviathan)—creates a deep sense of claustrophobia, existential dread, and alienation from superficial colonial society. When he finally emerges onto the empty deck at night, the subtext of his awe-struck description of the stars transforms the physical setting of the ship into a liminal, almost spiritual space, effectively preparing the reader for the mysterious undiscussed secret mentioned in the opening paragraph.
